final_proof:
Let \(\delta_n(x)=\dfrac{n}{\pi(1+n^2x^2)}\) for \(n\in\mathbb N_{>0}\). We first verify the usual delta-sequence properties. Each \(\delta_n\) is nonnegative and integrable. With the substitution \(u=nx\),
\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta_n(x)\,dx=\frac1\pi\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{du}{1+u^2}=\frac1\pi\bigl[\arctan u\bigr]_{-\infty}^{\infty}=1.
\]
Furthermore, for every \(\varepsilon>0\),
\[
\int_{|x|\geq\varepsilon}\delta_n(x)\,dx=\frac1\pi\int_{|u|\geq n\varepsilon}\frac{du}{1+u^2}=1-\frac2\pi\arctan(n\varepsilon)\longrightarrow 0,
\]
since \(\arctan(n\varepsilon)\to\pi/2\). Thus each function has total mass one, is nonnegative, and its mass outside every neighborhood of the origin tends to zero. Hence \((\delta_n)\) is a delta sequence.

We now prove the asserted distributional convergence. Let \(\phi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R)=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)\). Substituting \(u=nx\) gives
\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta_n(x)\phi(x)\,dx=\frac1\pi\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\phi(u/n)}{1+u^2}\,du.
\]
For every fixed \(u\in\mathbb R\), continuity of \(\phi\) at zero implies \(\phi(u/n)\to\phi(0)\). Also, because a compactly supported continuous function is bounded,
\[
\left|\frac1\pi\frac{\phi(u/n)}{1+u^2}\right|\leq\frac{\|\phi\|_\infty}{\pi(1+u^2)}.
\]
The right-hand side is integrable over \(\mathbb R\), and it is independent of \(n\). Therefore the dominated convergence theorem yields
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta_n(x)\phi(x)\,dx=\frac{\phi(0)}\pi\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{du}{1+u^2}=\phi(0).
\]
By definition, the Dirac delta distribution satisfies \(\langle\delta,\phi\rangle=\phi(0)\). Consequently \(\delta_n\to\delta\) in \(\mathcal D'(\mathbb R)\), as claimed.
